# **CHAPTER 1**

**INTRODUCTION**

## **Rationale of the Study**

Student governance and student representation remain fundamental components of higher education because they provide formal mechanisms through which students participate in institutional decision-making, advocate for student welfare, and collaborate with university administrators in strengthening institutional governance and campus development (Matthews & Dollinger, 2023; Patrick, 2023). Across higher education institutions worldwide, these representative bodies commonly operate as student councils, student governments, student unions, or similar organizations that promote student leadership, coordinate student activities, encourage civic participation, and represent student interests within institutional governance (Matthews & Dollinger, 2023; Patrick, 2023). In Philippine higher education institutions, Student Body Organizations (SBOs) commonly serve as the representative bodies of the student population, which perform operational responsibilities that include managing organizational finances, planning and implementing student activities, facilitating elections, disseminating organizational announcements, coordinating student-centered programs, and supporting organizational administration in accordance with institutional policies. As higher education institutions continue to undergo digital transformation, universities increasingly adopt integrated information systems to streamline administrative processes, strengthen organizational transparency, improve governance, and enhance institutional efficiency through technology-enabled solutions (Fernández et al., 2023; Gkrimpizi et al., 2023; Pei & Li, 2026). Likewise, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded institutional capabilities by supporting intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making that improve organizational planning, resource allocation, governance, and administrative effectiveness within higher education institutions (Misra et al., 2026; Bacalso et al., 2026; Nnaji et al., 2026). As these digital and AI-driven technologies continue to mature, they offer higher education institutions significant opportunities to strengthen student governance, improve organizational management, and promote more efficient, transparent, and evidence-based administrative processes.&nbsp;&nbsp;

Despite the increasing digital transformation of higher education institutions, student governance organizations across universities continue to face persistent structural, operational, and data management challenges that affect efficiency, accountability, and continuity. At the international level, studies on higher education governance indicate that student governance structures often experience fragmented governance systems, where records, communication, and administrative documents are stored across multiple unintegrated platforms, resulting in duplication of information, inefficient workflows, and weak organizational coordination (Mujahidin et al., 2026; Cheong & Nyaupane, 2022). Another major issue is leadership turnover and institutional memory loss, in which outgoing student officers fail to adequately document procedures, decisions, and organizational workflows, causing incoming officers to restart administrative processes rather than build on previous governance initiatives (Mutya, 2025; Ntando et al., 2026). This issue disrupts organizational continuity and weakens long-term organizational effectiveness. In addition, student governments often lack data-driven decision-making systems to effectively analyze participation trends, financial utilization, and organizational performance, leading governance decisions to rely more on assumptions than on empirical evidence (Biondi & Russo, 2022; Tfaily, 2026). Furthermore, student leaders experience considerable administrative workload as they balance academic responsibilities with governance duties, resulting in delays in documentation, reporting, communication, and coordination of organizational activities (Arca, 2026; Mutya, 2025). Another critical issue is limited financial transparency, in which stakeholders have difficulty monitoring budget allocations and expenditures due to inadequate financial management and internal control mechanisms, thereby reducing accountability and trust in governance structures (Alarcon et al., 2026; Mutya, 2025).

&nbsp;At the national level, particularly in the Philippines, similar governance challenges are evident across student organizations in various higher education institutions, including State Universities and Colleges (SUCs). Governance practices continue to face issues with administrative efficiency, transparency, and accountability, which affect organizational effectiveness (Mohammad, 2025; Aquino, 2025). One of the most common concerns is manual financial management, in which student organizations continue to rely on spreadsheets and paper-based liquidation reports, making financial monitoring and reporting time-consuming and error-prone (Alarcon et al., 2026; Aquino, 2025). Communication fragmentation is also a significant issue, as announcements and organizational updates are distributed across multiple digital platforms, including Messenger, Facebook, and email, resulting in inconsistent information dissemination and reduced coordination among members (Cheong & Nyaupane, 2022; Mohammad, 2025). In addition, documentation standardization remains a challenge because reports, proposals, and accomplishment records are often prepared using different formats without a centralized management system, making compliance monitoring and organizational auditing more difficult (Mujahidin et al., 2026; Mohammad, 2025). Another concern is the limited use of performance analytics tools to evaluate the effectiveness of student organizations in terms of participation, budget utilization, and project outcomes, thereby restricting evidence-based governance and strategic planning (Biondi & Russo, 2022; Tfaily, 2026). Furthermore, organizational approval workflows remain largely manual and require multiple levels of authorization, contributing to delays in the approval of activities, projects, and financial requests (Mujahidin et al., 2026; Aquino, 2025).

&nbsp;At the local level, Student Body Organizations (SBOs) in higher education institutions such as those operating in environments similar to the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue (UCLM), Cebu Technological University (CTU), and University of San Carlos (USC) experience governance and operational constraints comparable to those reported in higher education institutions nationally and internationally. One major issue is the workload overload experienced by student officers, in which a single officer often handles multiple administrative responsibilities across finance, documentation, events, and communication, increasing the likelihood of delays and human error (Arca, 2026; Mutya, 2025). Another challenge is decentralized record storage, in which organizational documents are maintained across personal devices, email accounts, and cloud storage platforms, making information retrieval inefficient and increasing the risk of data loss (Mujahidin et al., 2026; Cheong & Nyaupane, 2022). This issue becomes more evident during leadership transitions, when incoming officers struggle to obtain complete organizational records, resulting in repeated processes and the loss of institutional knowledge (Ntando et al., 2026; Mutya, 2025). In addition, SBOs often lack real-time financial visibility, preventing officers from accurately monitoring available budgets, pending reimbursements, and actual expenditures, thereby affecting financial decision-making (Alarcon et al., 2026). Organizational performance tracking also remains limited, as student governments rarely utilize structured indicators to evaluate participation, project implementation efficiency, and organizational impact, restricting opportunities for continuous improvement (Biondi & Russo, 2022; Tfaily, 2026). Lastly, student governance organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue continue to experience weak institutional memory because they do not consistently document governance practices, procedural guidelines, supplier information, and organizational records.(Mutya, 2025; Ntando et al., 2026).

&nbsp;Recent studies suggest that addressing the persistent challenges of budget opacity and errors associated with manual financial liquidation requires the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven financial management systems and digital ledger technologies. AI-enabled financial forecasting, automated reconciliation, and intelligent budgeting tools improve the accuracy of financial reporting, facilitate early detection of financial risks, and support evidence-based decision-making. Likewise, digital ledger systems provide secure, transparent, and real-time recording of financial transactions, reducing dependence on paper-based documentation while strengthening accountability and financial governance within higher education institutions (Zang, 2022; Kuyumdzhiev & Andreeva, 2022). These intelligent financial technologies enable organizations to proactively monitor expenditures, minimize human errors, and improve budget transparency throughout organizational operations.

&nbsp;Beyond financial management, intelligent workflow automation and integrated digital communication platforms have proven effective in reducing administrative workload and improving coordination among organizational members. By centralizing documentation, automating routine administrative processes, and preserving organizational records, these systems minimize fragmentation in communication and institutional memory loss while enhancing collaboration and continuity of governance across student organizations (Mujahidin et al., 2026; Jayaram & Bhat, 2022). Similarly, implementing biometric attendance systems has addressed the inefficiencies and security vulnerabilities associated with manual attendance recording and proxy participation. Biometric technology, including fingerprint and facial recognition, delivers precise, verifiable, and tamper-resistant attendance records while reducing administrative burden and improving accountability during academic and organizational activities (Sultana & Akter, 2025; Adebisi et al., 2026).

&nbsp;Establishing secure electronic voting systems has likewise addressed the challenges associated with manual election processes by improving the integrity, accessibility, and transparency of student elections. Secure online voting platforms that utilize user authentication, encrypted communication, digital verification, and automated vote counting provide accurate and efficient election management while protecting voter privacy and reducing opportunities for electoral fraud. These systems also eliminate repetitive manual tabulation and accelerate the generation of election results, thereby promoting greater trust and accountability in campus elections (Jafar et al., 2022; Revelo Sánchez et al., 2026).

Finally, implementing digital inventory management integrated with automated queue management has significantly improved merchandise distribution and the management of organizational resources. These intelligent systems enable organizations to monitor inventory levels in real time, accurately verify transactions, efficiently organize participant queues, and reduce congestion during distribution activities. Consequently, they improve operational efficiency, strengthen accountability, and ensure accurate fulfillment of merchandise requests (Jayaram & Bhat, 2022; Mujahidin et al., 2026).

&nbsp;In response to the persistent challenges in student governance and financial management, as well as the limitations of existing solutions, this study proposes HIUSA: an AI-integrated Student Governance and Financial Management System. While previous systems have improved specific functions such as financial management, workflow automation, attendance monitoring, and online voting, they often operate as standalone solutions that lack integration and intelligent decision-support capabilities. As a result, student organizations continue to experience fragmented workflows, manual administrative processes, limited financial insights, and difficulties in maintaining organizational continuity during leadership transitions.  
&nbsp;To address these gaps, HIUSA integrates key governance functions into a single platform, including an Automated Digital Ledger, biometric attendance tracking using the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader, secure online voting, tokenized merchandise queuing, dynamic inventory management, centralized document management, and comprehensive event management. The system also incorporates an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression model for financial forecasting, a Budget Advisory System that combines OLS forecast outputs with predefined financial rules to recommend responsible budget utilization, a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm for intelligent officer task delegation, and a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API to support AI-assisted functions such as organizational announcement drafting, the AI-assisted Event Planning Assistant for generating structured event preparation guidance, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) that produces clear, human-readable explanations of AI-assisted forecasts, recommendations, and budget advisories.  
&nbsp;Unlike conventional student governance systems, HIUSA combines operational management, financial administration, and AI-driven decision support into a single centralized platform. It also provides interactive dashboards, organizational analytics, and actionable insights that enable student officers and faculty advisers to make informed decisions, improve transparency, reduce administrative workload, and strengthen continuity in student governance. In addition, HIUSA uses the Groq-powered LLM to generate financial reports from financial data and fetch the OLS forecast outputs, allowing the system to present projected income, projected expenses, and related financial trends in a more organized, readable, and interpretable format. Through this feature, the system not only presents numerical forecast results but also transforms them into structured financial reports that can support clearer communication, easier financial review, and more informed budget planning within student organizations.  
&nbsp;The primary goal of this study is to analyze, design, and develop Hiusa as a centralized governance platform for student body organizations at the University of Cebu in Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. Specifically, the study aims to identify SBOs' current student governance and financial management processes and the problems encountered in its fragmented workflow. Furthermore, the study seeks to determine the specific mechanisms and techniques that the Hiusa system will use, particularly for AI-driven financial forecasting, real-time budget risk advisory, automated digital ledger recording, and dynamic budget allocation. It also focuses on integrating intelligent officer task delegation, automated event planning workflows, and biometric attendance tracking to streamline daily operations. Crucially, the research will establish the technical foundations for secure online voting and tokenized merchandise queuing, ensuring dynamic inventory tracking and rigorous order-fulfillment verification. By defining and developing the best features of this proposed AI-integrated system, the study will ultimately evaluate its acceptability among end users. Through these objectives, this research intends to deliver a permanent, highly functional system that eliminates the repetitive labor of past administrations and sets a new standard for operational excellence.

## **Objectives of the Study**

**General Objective**

The objective of this research is to analyze, design, develop, test, and evaluate a student body organization management system that utilizes AI-integrated digital functionalities to help student body organizations at the University of Cebu – Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue improve financial management, event and task coordination, elections, merchandise management, and organizational communication through a centralized and systematic platform.

**Specific Objectives**

Specifically, the study will:

1. Identify and assess the current student governance and financial management practices of student body organizations at the University of Cebu – Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue in accordance with:&nbsp;  
   1. processes, and  
   2. problems encountered.  
2. Determine the mechanisms or techniques to be utilized for the AI \- integrated student governance and financial management system concerning:&nbsp;  
   1. financial management,  
   2. event management,  
   3. task management,  
   4. elections,  
   5. merchandise management, and  
   6. organizational communication.&nbsp;  
3. Define and develop the best features of the proposed AI-integrated student governance and  financial management system.&nbsp;  
4. Evaluate the level of acceptability of the proposed system.&nbsp;

**Scope and Limitations of the Study**

This study aims to improve the organization's management of student governance, financial operations, event coordination, merchandise transactions, and student elections by developing HIUSA: An AI-Integrated Student Governance and Financial Management System for Student Body Organizations (SBO) of the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue (UCLM). The study's goal is to support more organized processes, improve transparency, reduce manual work, and provide timely information to help SBO officers make decisions, all while increasing student accessibility and participation.

&nbsp;The functional scope of Hiusa includes integrated modules that support governance, financial operations, event coordination, merchandise services, and election activities within student body organizations. The system centralizes organizational processes that are traditionally handled manually and provides digital support for daily organizational operations. However, the platform focuses only on processes directly related to student governance and organizational management and does not attempt to replace institutional administrative systems or university-wide management platforms.

&nbsp;The artificial intelligence capabilities of HIUSA consist of both internally implemented analytical models and externally integrated generative AI services. Internally, the system employs an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression model to analyze historical financial transactions and forecast future income and expenditure trends, supporting financial planning through the Budget Advisory System, which generates spending recommendations based on forecast outputs and current budget allocations. HIUSA also implements a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm that evaluates predefined organizational criteria, including officer roles, workload, and availability, to generate ranked recommendations for task delegation. These analytical components are developed directly within the system and do not rely on external machine learning frameworks. For natural language processing tasks, HIUSA integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) via the Groq API to provide AI-assisted announcement drafting, financial report summarization, and an Event Planning Assistant that generates recommended timelines, logistics checklists, and resource suggestions based on user-provided event information. The same LLM also supports Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) by transforming outputs from the OLS forecasting model, Budget Advisory System, and Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm into human-readable explanations that improve the transparency and interpretability of AI-assisted recommendations.&nbsp;

&nbsp;One major scope of the system is financial management. HIUSA provides digital tools for recording financial transactions, monitoring organizational funds, generating financial reports, managing budget allocations for projects and activities, maintaining a centralized digital ledger, and automatically issuing digital receipts for completed transactions. To support financial planning, the system incorporates an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression model that analyzes historical financial records to forecast future income and expenditure trends. The Budget Advisory System utilizes these forecast results to generate AI-assisted spending recommendations and proposed budget allocations based on projected financial conditions. To improve transparency and interpretability, the system also applies Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) through a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed via the Groq API, which converts forecast outputs and budget recommendations into human-readable explanations for officers and advisers. These AI-assisted outputs are intended solely to support organizational decision-making and should not replace the judgment of officers, advisers, or other authorized organizational officials. Furthermore, the accuracy and reliability of the forecasting and budget advisory functions depend on the availability, completeness, and quality of the historical financial data stored within the system. During the initial stages of implementation, limited historical financial records may reduce the accuracy and consistency of the forecasts and budget recommendations generated.&nbsp;

&nbsp;Another major scope of the system is event and task management. HIUSA provides tools for event planning, activity scheduling, workflow automation, task coordination, attendance monitoring, event budget monitoring, and automated notifications to improve organizational operations and communication. To support organizational planning, the system incorporates a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm that generates recommendations for officer task delegation by evaluating predefined organizational criteria, including officer roles, workload, and availability. In addition, an AI-assisted Event Planning Assistant, powered by a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API, generates recommended event timelines, logistics checklists, resource suggestions, and preparation plans based on user-provided event information. These AI-assisted recommendations are intended solely to support organizational planning and decision-making, while final decisions remain the responsibility of officers and advisers. Attendance monitoring supports both digital and biometric verification. The biometric attendance feature utilizes the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader for real-time identity verification and depends on proper device configuration and stable system connectivity. Organizations without compatible biometric hardware may continue using the system's standard digital attendance functionality.&nbsp;

&nbsp;The system also includes a merchandise management component to improve inventory monitoring, order processing, and product distribution. Students may access merchandise information, utilizes the tokenized queue system in placing reservations or making purchases, choose between supported payment options such as e-wallet payments (specifically GCash) and cash on claim, receive digital claim references, and monitor order progress through the system. Officers are provided with inventory monitoring, order management, payment verification, and fulfillment functions to support organized release procedures. However, inventory accuracy remains dependent on administrative updates and actual stock recording practices. Although the merchandise component supports hybrid payment methods and organizational transaction monitoring, it only supports GCash and Cash on Claim as payment options. It does not support additional payment options beyond those implemented during deployment.&nbsp;&nbsp;

The system also includes digital voting and election management functions to support student participation during election periods. The platform supports election administration, candidate management, vote monitoring, and automated tallying, while implementing mechanisms to minimize duplicate voting and unauthorized access. However, the system is limited to organizational-level elections and does not replace official university election procedures, institutional policies, or validation requirements. Election integrity also depends on responsible account usage, proper implementation of verification procedures, and active student participation. The system does not independently verify voter identity beyond the authentication and access controls implemented within the platform.

The platform implements role-based access control through four user roles: Administrator, Department Head, SBO Member, and Student. The Administrator role includes the SBO Adviser, President, Secretary, Treasurer, Auditor, Chief of Development (where applicable), and other authorized officers with administrative privileges. Administrators can manage user accounts, organizational records, system configurations, access permissions, financial transactions, organizational events, inventory, merchandise distribution, elections, workflow processes, and AI-assisted decision support tools. The Department Head role oversees Student Body Organizations within its respective department by reviewing financial records, monitoring events and organizational performance, supervising elections, and accessing reports and AI-generated recommendations to support informed decision-making. The platform assigns the SBO Member role to the remaining organization officers who do not have administrative privileges. SBO Members can oversee assigned organizational workflows, verify attendance, receive announcements and event notifications, monitor organizational activities, and access organization-related information necessary for their designated responsibilities. The platform assigns the Student role to currently enrolled students who access organization-related services, including participating in electronic voting, reserving merchandise, verifying attendance, receiving announcements and event notifications, and monitoring organizational activities. Access to system information and functionality is controlled by assigned user roles to maintain organizational security, data integrity, and operational control.&nbsp;

&nbsp;Despite its intended advantages, the proposed system has several limitations that define the study's scope. First, Hiusa is designed specifically for the operational structure, processes, and requirements of Student Body Organizations at the University of Cebu, Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. As such, implementation in other student organizations' campuses or institutions may require modifications to workflows, policies, organizational structures, and user access configurations. Second, the effectiveness of AI-supported functions, including financial forecasting, budget advisory, workflow recommendations, event planning assistance, and task delegation, is dependent on the quality, availability, and consistency of historical and operational data. During early deployment stages, limited records may affect the accuracy and reliability of generated recommendations. Therefore, users should interpret AI-generated outputs as supportive guidance rather than treat them as final organizational decisions. Third, the system requires internet connectivity and compatible digital devices to function properly. Users experiencing unstable network access may encounter delays in synchronization, notifications, attendance updates, election participation, and other real-time services. Certain advanced functions may also perform differently depending on device specifications and connectivity conditions. Fourth, the current implementation does not fully integrate with institutional systems, including official enrollment databases, student information systems, university accounting platforms, and external payment gateways. User account creation, validation, and operational records may initially require controlled registration and administrative verification procedures, depending on implementation readiness. Fifth, security controls are implemented to support voting integrity, financial transparency, and controlled access. However, the system cannot fully prevent misuse, human error, unauthorized actions, incorrect data entry, or external technical risks. The system minimizes operational issues through access controls, monitoring mechanisms, and verification procedures rather than eliminating all possible risks. Lastly, the development and implementation of Hiusa are limited to the timeframe, resources, and feasibility conditions of the capstone project. Although the system architecture supports future expansion and additional intelligent capabilities, the current implementation includes only the modules and functions defined within this study.

**Significance of the Study**

The study focuses on the potential benefits it offers to the academic community of the University of Cebu, Lapu-Lapu, and Mandaue through the development and implementation of Hiusa: An AI-Integrated Student Governance and Financial Management System. This study aims to benefit the following groups through its findings and outcomes.

**SBO Officers and Advisers**.  These stakeholders benefit directly from the system's ability to streamline the processes identified in the study's objectives. Officers are relieved of the burden of manual accounting and event planning through Hiusa's AI-driven financial ledgers and automated event workflows. SBO advisers gain actionable insights into the organization's financial health and operational performance through real-time analytics, enabling more effective mentorship and oversight of the society's financial and administrative activities.  
&nbsp;**Student Body Organizations (SBO).** As the organization targeted for system development, SBOs transitioned from manual, fragmented record-keeping to a centralized, digital platform. Hiusa archives the society's financial history, event workflows, and election records in a permanent database. The implementation of the system prevents the loss of institutional knowledge that occurs during leadership transitions, ensuring long-term continuity, reliable organizational records, and increased credibility for the society.

**University of Cebu, Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue.** This study benefits the university by showcasing a practical application of technology within its administrative framework. Hiusa serves as a pilot project, demonstrating how Artificial Intelligence integrates into campus operations. By automating governance tasks, the system offers a model for other departments to consider, potentially increasing efficiency and supporting the university's move toward a more digital and data-informed administrative environment.  
&nbsp;**Students.** The general student body gains access to a seamless, transparent, democratic, and transactional ecosystem. Through the secure online voting portal, students exercise their right to vote without the frustration of manual counting delays or security concerns. Furthermore, the tokenized merchandise queuing system and dynamic inventory tracking ensure that students have a convenient, digitized experience when accessing organizational services, eliminating the need to endure long lines or to verify order fulfillment.  
&nbsp;**Faculty.** Faculty members benefit from the enhanced data visibility and organizational maturity within the College. With Hiusa streamlining the society's operations, faculty members spend less time mediating administrative disputes or managing logistical hiccups, allowing for a more productive environment focused on academic development and collaborative research projects between the faculty and the student body.  
&nbsp;**Researchers.** The current research team benefits by gaining practical experience in software engineering and AI integration, successfully navigating the complexities of designing a system that meets the specific administrative needs of an academic society. This study provides the researchers with a documented technical roadmap for solving real-world governance problems through intelligent automation and AI-driven forecasting.  
&nbsp;**Future Researchers.** Future scholars may use this study as a benchmark for developing more advanced AI-based governance platforms. The findings, design framework, and implementation of Hiusa can guide further exploration into digital democratic systems, intelligent workflow automation, and the practical application of AI-integrated management tools in higher education, contributing to the continuous evolution of technology-enhanced governance.&nbsp;

## **DEFINITION OF TERMS**

This section presents the terminology used in this study and explains its corresponding applications:

| AI-Driven Financial Forecasting \- The implementation of an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression model within the Finance module of Hiusa to evaluate historical SBO transaction data and generate quantitative forecasts of future income, expenses, and budget capacity for organizational planning and decision-making.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| :---- | ----- |
| **Automated Accounting \-** The systematic, real-time electronic capture, categorization, and storage of SBO financial transactions through the Finance module of Hiusa, replacing manual ledger entry and ensuring that all income and expense records are immediately accessible and auditable.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **AI-assisted Event Planning Assistant –** An intelligent planning feature within the Events module of Hiusa that utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API to generate structured event preparation plans, recommended timelines, logistics checklists, task lists, and planning guidance based on user-provided event details, including the event type, schedule, expected participants, venue, and allocated budget.&nbsp; |  |
| **Biometric Attendance Tracking** – A fingerprint-based attendance verification feature implemented within the Events module of HIUSA that utilizes the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader to authenticate the identity of participating students in real time. Upon successful verification, the system automatically records attendance and synchronizes tamper-resistant attendance records with the centralized database, improving the accuracy, security, and efficiency of event participation monitoring.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Budget Advisory System** – An AI-assisted decision-support component within the Finance module of Hiusa that analyzes Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) financial forecasts together with current budget allocations and predefined financial rules to generate spending recommendations for SBO officers. The system also utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) via the Groq API to present these recommendations as clear, contextualized advisory messages that support informed financial decision-making.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Digital Voting Portal \-** The Elections module of Hiusa, which provides a web-based interface through which verified SBO members submit electronic ballots during officer elections, with role-based access controls ensuring that each authenticated user may cast exactly one vote per election period.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Digital Transformation \-** Replacing manual, paper-based governance and administrative workflows within SBO with the Hiusa platform's integrated digital processes enables centralized data management, automated reporting, and real-time organizational oversight.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Dynamic Budget Allocation \-** A feature of the Finance module of Hiusa that adjusts the distribution of available organizational funds across activity categories based on real-time expenditure data and projections generated by the OLS financial forecasting engine.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Dynamic Inventory Tracking \-** The real-time stock monitoring capability of Hiusa's Merchandise module continuously updates item quantities as orders are processed, triggers low-stock alerts when stock levels fall below predefined thresholds, and maintains synchronized records of all inventory movements.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Event Management System \-** The Events module of Hiusa provides SBO officers with tools to plan, schedule, assign personnel, monitor budgets, and track the execution status of campus activities. It integrates automated task generation and notification workflows.&nbsp; |  |
| **Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)** – It utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed via the Groq API to translate the outputs of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) forecasting model, the Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm, and the Budget Advisory System into clear and understandable explanations, enabling officers of student body organizations to interpret AI-assisted recommendations better and make informed decisions.&nbsp; |  |
| **Financial Management** – An integrated organizational function within Hiusa that manages the planning, allocation, monitoring, forecasting, and reporting of financial resources for Student Body Organization. It enables officers to record financial transactions, allocate budgets, forecast future income and expenditures using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, generate financial reports, and provide budget spending recommendations to support transparent, accountable, and evidence-based financial decision-making.&nbsp; |  |
| **HIUSA (AI-Integrated Student Governance and Financial Management System) \-** A web-based platform developed for different student body organizations in the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue that consolidates student governance operations, including financial management, event coordination, task delegation, merchandise fulfillment, and election administration, into a single integrated system. The name originates from the Cebuano word for unity.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Large Language Model API \-** An application programming interface (API) in the cloud that gives users access to a large language model that has already been trained and can comprehend and produce natural language text. In Hiusa, the Groq API is used to provide AI-assisted language generation for drafting organizational announcements and to support Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) by producing clear, human-readable explanations of AI-assisted forecasts, recommendations, and budget advisory outputs.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Order Fulfillment Verification \-** The step within the Merchandise module of Hiusa where an officer validates the digital claim token presented by the student, confirms that the student completed the purchase, and releases the corresponding merchandise item.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Ordinary Least Squares Linear Regression \-** A statistical technique implemented in the Finance module of Hiusa that models the linear relationship among time-based financial variables by reducing the squared differences between actual and estimated values and generates projections of future organizational income and expenditures.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Role-Based Access Control \-** A security model implemented throughout Hiusa that assigns each registered user one of four roles, namely Admin, Adviser, Officer, or Student, and restricts that user's system permissions to only the actions and data associated with their designated role.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm \-** A deterministic decision-support algorithm implemented in the Tasks module of Hiusa that scores each eligible officer against predefined weighted criteria, including current task load and role designation, and returns a ranked recommendation list to guide officer task delegation decisions.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Student Body Organization (SBO) \-** A formally recognized student governance entity within a higher education institution that manages organizational operations, funds, and activities. In this study, the term refers to the recognized college-level student organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue.&nbsp; |  |
| **Tokenized Queue System \-** A fulfillment mechanism within the Merchandise module of Hiusa in which the system issues a unique alphanumeric claim token to a student after completing a merchandise reservation, and the student later presents the token to an officer for validation and merchandise release.&nbsp; |  |
| **Web-Based System \-** A software application delivered entirely through a standard web browser without requiring local installation. Hiusa is built on a React frontend and a Laravel backend, making it accessible to users across devices through a network connection.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
| **Workflow Automation \-** The Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm manages the automatic generation and assignment of tasks to SBO officers within the Tasks module of Hiusa, considering officer roles, existing workloads, and task requirements, without administrator intervention.&nbsp;&nbsp; |  |
