# **CHAPTER II**

**REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES**

This chapter presents the pertinent literary works, a conceptual framework, related studies, and a comparative matrix.&nbsp;

## **Related Literatures**&nbsp;

In this section, previously published academic works provide essential insights, theoretical foundations, research methodologies, and pertinent findings related to the research topic. By leveraging these established approaches and discoveries, this body of literature is instrumental in informing the development and execution of our study.&nbsp;

**Ordinary Least Squares Linear Regression**

Ordinary Least Squares, or OLS, is a way of studying how one factor changes in relation to one or more other factors. It creates a straight-line model from past data and checks how close the estimated values are to the actual results. The model then chooses the equation with the smallest total error. Because the results are easy to read and interpret, researchers often use OLS in financial studies, prediction, and other numerical analyses.

In international research, OLS continues to serve as a common starting point for studying financial patterns and economic data. Researchers often choose it because the output is clear and can easily show whether one variable has a positive, negative, or weak connection with another. Hjalmarsson and Kiss (2022) used OLS in a study involving long-term predictive regression. Their work showed that the method can help assess whether past financial information is meaningfully related to future results over a given period.

Researchers in the Philippines have also used OLS to study business performance and financial conditions. Caboverde (2022) applied the method to examine whether environmental rules and compliance requirements affected the profit growth of small and medium-sized businesses. The study included firms from Metro Manila, Metro Cebu, and Metro Davao. Using OLS, the researcher compared the level of regulatory pressure experienced by the businesses with changes in their financial performance. The findings showed that the method could provide understandable numerical estimates for real business situations. The study also suggests that OLS remains useful in local studies that involve financial records, company performance, and decisions about organizational resources.  
&nbsp;HIUSA uses Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression within its Financial Information System to assist Student Body Organizations in forecasting future financial performance. The model analyzes historical transaction records stored in the Automated Digital Ledger to identify trends in organizational income and expenses over time. To estimate the regression line, the system first computes the slope using the formula b₁ \= Σ\[(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)\] / Σ(x − x̄)², where b₁ is the regression coefficient (slope), x represents the predictor variable (such as the transaction period), x̄ is the mean of the predictor values, y is the observed financial value (such as income or expense), and ȳ is the mean of the observed financial values. The model calculates the intercept using b₀ \= ȳ − b₁x̄, where b₀ represents the baseline financial value when the predictor variable is zero. After determining the regression coefficients, the system generates forecasts using the prediction equation ŷ \= b₀ \+ b₁x, where ŷ is the predicted financial value for a given transaction period. The OLS method fits a regression model by reducing the squared prediction errors, expressed as  Σ(y − ŷ)², allowing the predicted financial values to match the observed values closely. Based on the resulting regression model, HIUSA projects future income and expense trends to support budget planning, financial forecasting, and evidence-based organizational decision-making. The generated forecasts are supplied to the Budget Advisory System to produce budget allocation and spending recommendations based on projected financial conditions. In addition, both the historical transaction records maintained in the Automated Digital Ledger and the forecasting results generated by the OLS model are utilized by the Groq-powered Large Language Model (LLM) to automatically generate human-readable financial reports, including income statements, expense summaries, audit logs, financial summaries, and event-specific financial reports. These reports consolidate recorded financial transactions with AI-generated forecasting insights. The system may export them in PDF and Excel formats to support financial monitoring, documentation, auditing, and organizational reporting.&nbsp;

**Rule-Based Decision-Making with Weighted Scoring**

Rule-based decision-making with weighted scoring is a deterministic decision-support approach that combines predefined organizational rules with weighted evaluation criteria to recommend the most appropriate course of action. The approach incorporates expert system principles by representing organizational knowledge through explicit rules and applying rule-based inference to identify eligible alternatives. It also applies multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to evaluate and rank those alternatives based on multiple weighted criteria. Unlike machine learning techniques that learn from historical data, rule-based decision-making follows predefined logic, producing transparent, consistent, and explainable recommendations. Because the approach bases every decision on organizational policies and measurable evaluation criteria, it provides objective, auditable decision support, making it particularly suitable for environments where task delegation and organizational accountability are essential.

Globally, rule-based decision support, combined with multi-criteria evaluation, has become an effective approach to producing transparent and objective organizational recommendations. Zhu et al. (2022) proposed a rule-based decision support framework that integrates Variable Precision Rough Set theory with Stochastic Multi-Objective Acceptability Analysis to improve multi-attribute decision-making. Their study demonstrated that extracting explicit decision rules and combining them with weighted evaluation enables efficient ranking of alternatives while reducing unnecessary evaluation effort. Likewise, Chen and Utama (2022) developed a decision-support model that integrates fuzzy logic with the Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) method to evaluate employees based on multiple weighted criteria. Their findings demonstrated that weighted decision models can objectively rank alternatives and support consistent personnel selection by reducing subjectivity in organizational decision-making. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that combining rule-based reasoning with multi-criteria evaluation provides a transparent, systematic, and reliable foundation for organizational decision support.&nbsp;&nbsp;

Globally, expert systems have remained a relevant rule-based approach for supporting transparent and consistent decision-making in complex environments. Regueras et al. (2022) developed a rule-based expert system to certify teachers’ competence in using Learning Management Systems by deriving classification rules from LMS activity data. Using records from 3,303 courses and approximately two million interactive events, the study showed that the system could automatically and satisfactorily evaluate teacher competence, with validation results indicating successful performance relative to expert judgment. Their findings suggest that expert systems can formalize domain knowledge into explicit rules and apply those rules consistently to support reliable decision-making at scale. Likewise, Casal-Guisande et al. (2022) proposed an expert-system-based decision-making methodology for monitoring machining tool conditions, combining a rule-based knowledge base with fuzzy inference and hierarchization methods. Their study found that the methodology could detect undesirable operating conditions, reduce errors, help prevent harmful failures and accidents, and generate savings in time and cost while improving operational performance. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that expert systems provide a strong foundation for decision support by transforming expert knowledge into explicit rules, applying those rules systematically, and producing consistent, interpretable, and practical recommendations across domains.&nbsp;

Within the Philippine context, recent studies likewise demonstrate the effectiveness of rule-based decision support systems in automating evaluation processes and producing consistent recommendations. Alix et al. (2022) developed a faculty evaluation system incorporating a decision support mechanism that automatically generated faculty development plans based on evaluation results. Their study showed that integrating rule-based decision support improved consistency and reduced manual analysis in organizational decision-making. Similarly, Alvaran et al. (2022) designed a web-based performance evaluation system that used a rule-based algorithm to analyze assessment results and automatically recommend appropriate learning materials based on predefined evaluation rules. Their findings demonstrated that rule-based logic can consistently generate objective recommendations while minimizing human intervention during evaluation processes. Together, these studies indicate that rule-based decision support systems provide an effective foundation for automating organizational recommendations within educational institutions.&nbsp;

Local researchers have likewise applied weighted decision-making approaches to support objective evaluation and organizational decision-making. Yamagishi et al. (2022), researchers from Cebu Technological University and the University of San Carlos, developed an evaluation framework that integrated the Fuzzy Best–Worst Method (FBWM) and Fuzzy Simple Additive Weighting (FSAW) to assess the performance of small-island tourism destinations using multiple weighted criteria. Their findings demonstrated that weighted scoring methods provide a systematic and transparent approach for evaluating alternatives and generating objective rankings despite multiple decision factors. Although the study focused on tourism management, it highlights the effectiveness of weighted multi-criteria evaluation in supporting evidence-based decision-making.&nbsp;

In alignment with these findings, Hiusa incorporates a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm within its Tasks Module to support officer task delegation. The algorithm first applies predefined organizational rules to determine officer eligibility based on criteria such as role designation, officer availability, and organizational policies. Only officers who satisfy these conditions proceed to the scoring stage. The system then computes a weighted score using the formula FinalScore \= (RoleWeight × RoleScore) \+ (WorkloadWeight × WorkloadScore) \+ (PerformanceWeight × PerformanceScore), where RoleWeight, WorkloadWeight, and PerformanceWeight represent the relative importance assigned to each decision criterion, while RoleScore, WorkloadScore, and PerformanceScore represent an officer's suitability based on their role compatibility, current workload, and historical task performance, respectively. The resulting FinalScore serves as the basis for ranking eligible officers, with the officer obtaining the highest score being recommended for task assignment.&nbsp;

**Large Language Models**

Large Language Models (LLMs) function as advanced artificial intelligence systems that comprehend, generate, and transform human language. They are trained on large-scale textual datasets, enabling them to learn linguistic structures, contextual relationships, and semantic patterns. As a result, LLMs can perform various natural language processing tasks, including text summarization, content generation, translation, and question answering. Their ability to produce coherent and context-aware responses has led to their widespread adoption in systems that require automated writing and information processing. In organizational environments, LLMs enhance communication efficiency by supporting administrative documentation tasks, such as generating reports, announcements, and other written communications.

Globally, recent research has shown that Large Language Models are highly effective at summarizing and generating structured text from complex documents. Zhang et al. (2024) conducted a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs for news summarization. They found that instruction-tuned LLMs can produce high-quality summaries comparable to human-written outputs, particularly in terms of coherence and informativeness. Similarly, Liu et al. (2024) introduced an LLM-as-reference learning framework for summarization tasks. They demonstrated that LLM-generated summaries can significantly improve downstream summarization performance and serve as reliable sources for compressing long-form content. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that LLMs are effective tools for condensing information and generating structured outputs, making them suitable for applications involving document summarization and automated content generation.

Globally, recent research has shown that Large Language Models can strengthen Explainable Artificial Intelligence by converting technical model outputs into clear and human-readable explanations. Zytek et al. (2024) developed Explingo, an LLM-based framework that transforms explanations from established XAI techniques, such as SHAP, into natural-language narratives. The researchers evaluated the generated explanations based on accuracy, completeness, fluency, and conciseness and reported strong performance, particularly when they guided the LLM with human-labeled and automatically generated examples. Similarly, Martens et al. (2025) developed XAIstories, a framework that uses LLMs to convert SHAP values and counterfactual explanations into narrative descriptions of how AI models produce predictions. Their user evaluation showed that more than 90% of the participants considered the SHAP-based narratives convincing, while more than 78% viewed the counterfactual narratives as convincing in the tabular-data experiment.&nbsp;&nbsp;

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, recent studies indicate growing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence tools in higher education, particularly for academic writing, summarization, and content generation. Goli-Cruz (2024) examined faculty perceptions of ChatGPT use in Philippine higher education and found that educators recognized its usefulness in supporting academic tasks such as drafting, explaining concepts, and improving written outputs, while also noting concerns about accuracy and the responsible use of AI tools. Similarly, Obenza et al. (2024) investigated university students' perception and use of ChatGPT in a Philippine university context. They reported that students frequently use generative AI tools to assist in writing, idea generation, and summarizing academic content, highlighting its role as a productivity-enhancing tool in academic workflows. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that in the Philippine educational setting, LLM-based tools are increasingly integrated into academic practices to support writing and information processing tasks, reinforcing their relevance in systems that require automated summarization and structured content generation.

Higher education institutions within the local context have likewise explored the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support written communication. Suico et al. (2025) examined the use of ChatGPT to enhance students' essay-writing skills in purposive communication at the University of Cebu–Maritime Education and Training Center. The study found that ChatGPT effectively assisted users in generating coherent, organized, and contextually appropriate written content, demonstrating its potential to improve writing efficiency and communication quality. Although the study focused on academic writing rather than organizational management, its findings provide relevant support for implementing a Large Language Model at HIUSA, where the Groq API is used to assist officers in drafting organizational announcements and generating clear, human-readable explanations of AI-assisted system outputs.&nbsp;

In alignment with these findings, HIUSA integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API to support AI-assisted language generation across multiple organizational functions. Within the Announcements module, the LLM assists officers in drafting organizational announcements from user-provided information. The LLM also powers the AI-assisted Event Planning Assistant, generating structured event-preparation timelines, planning guidance, resource recommendations, and task checklists based on user-provided event details. In addition, the LLM supports the Financial Information System by automatically generating human-readable financial reports, including income statements, expense summaries, audit logs, financial summaries, and event-specific financial reports derived from recorded organizational transactions and the outputs of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) financial forecasting model. These reports consolidate historical financial records and AI-generated forecasts into comprehensive summaries that the system can export in PDF and Excel formats to support financial documentation, auditing, and organizational decision-making. Furthermore, the LLM supports Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) by translating the outputs of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) forecasting model, the Budget Advisory System, and the Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm into clear, human-readable explanations, thereby improving transparency, communication efficiency, and informed decision-making.&nbsp;

**Financial Information Systems**&nbsp;

Transitioning to a centralized digital financial-tracking environment is essential for student organizations seeking to improve transparency and eliminate risks associated with budget mismanagement. Financial Information Systems (FIS) are integrated information systems designed to support the planning, recording, processing, monitoring, and reporting of an organization's financial activities. By centralizing financial data and automating core financial processes, FIS enables organizations to maintain accurate financial records, monitor income and expenditures in real time, enforce budget controls, and generate timely financial reports that support informed decision-making. The integration of digital ledger technologies further strengthens financial governance by ensuring that financial transactions are systematically recorded, securely stored, and readily accessible for auditing and accountability. Collectively, these capabilities reduce dependence on manual bookkeeping practices while promoting financial transparency, operational efficiency, and responsible resource management.&nbsp;

Globally, existing literature emphasizes that implementing structured digital financial systems is critical to maintaining institutional financial integrity. Uleh et al. (2025) found that organizations utilizing digital financial reporting systems are better able to allocate resources efficiently, minimize financial risks, and strengthen stakeholder trust through improved transparency. Similarly, Darteh (2023) highlighted that automated budgeting and financial execution systems reduce inconsistencies associated with manual tracking and contribute to long-term financial sustainability. These findings collectively suggest that digital financial systems are not merely tools for efficiency but foundational mechanisms for ensuring disciplined and transparent financial governance within structured organizations.&nbsp;

In the Philippine context, studies reveal persistent challenges in financial management stemming from the continued reliance on manual accounting systems within student organizations. Alba et al. (2026) identified limitations in financial forecasting, documentation accuracy, and analytical reporting among student councils, which they attributed primarily to manual processes and a lack of automation. Likewise, Gingrich and Qu (2024) reported that inadequate financial systems contribute to inefficient resource allocation, making it difficult for student leaders to manage organizational funds and meet operational objectives properly. These findings indicate that the absence of structured financial tools significantly constrains financial accuracy and governance effectiveness in student-led institutions.

Within the local context, recent Cebu-based literature likewise highlights the importance of transparent and systematically monitored financial management in strengthening governance and improving budget execution. Salvador et al. (2025) examined fiscal transparency and disbursement efficiency in a local government unit in Cebu Province. They discovered a statistically significant positive correlation between efficiency and transparency in the execution of the quarterly budget. Their study emphasized that improved monitoring, structured reporting, and stronger fiscal discipline support more accountable and evidence-based resource allocation.&nbsp;&nbsp;

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates a Financial Information System (FIS) to strengthen financial governance among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The Finance module centralizes financial management by enabling officers to record and monitor organizational income and expenditures via an Automated Digital Ledger, manage budgets with the Budget Allocation Manager, and maintain digital receipts for every transaction. The system further enhances financial oversight through a centralized Transaction History Dashboard, auto-generated financial reports, and AI-assisted financial forecasting using the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression model, supporting proactive budget planning. In addition, the Budget Advisory System analyzes forecasted financial trends alongside current budget allocations to provide responsible spending recommendations before overspending occurs. By integrating these financial management capabilities into a unified platform, HIUSA improves financial transparency, accountability, accuracy, and evidence-based decision-making while reducing reliance on manual financial record-keeping.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;

**Event Management Systems**

&nbsp;Event Management Systems (EMS) are integrated information systems designed to support the planning, coordination, execution, and monitoring of organizational events through a centralized digital platform. These systems streamline event-related processes by managing schedules, participant information, resource allocation, budgeting, and communication within a unified environment. As event management technologies continue to evolve, researchers increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence to automate planning tasks, provide intelligent recommendations, and improve decision-making throughout the event lifecycle. By integrating AI-assisted functionalities with conventional event management processes, organizations can reduce administrative workload, minimize scheduling conflicts, and improve the efficiency, accuracy, and coordination of campus activities.&nbsp;

Globally, literature indicates that artificial intelligence significantly enhances the efficiency and reliability of event management processes. Surya (2026) found that integrating AI into event portals improves operational efficiency by automating fragmented processes, such as booking systems and inquiry management. The study further emphasized that centralized intelligent platforms enhance decision-making, improve service delivery, and streamline coordination among stakeholders. In addition, AI-driven tools such as chatbots and automated notification systems reduce human error, accelerate response times, and enable faster and more reliable event processing. These findings suggest that AI-enabled event systems are increasingly becoming essential tools for improving the scalability and efficiency of complex event operations.

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, studies similarly demonstrate that digital transformation in event management leads to measurable improvements in organizational performance. Agpalo et al. (2025) found that implementing a web-based event management system significantly improved administrative efficiency by replacing manual tracking with a centralized digital platform. The study reported high user satisfaction, including a 4.85/5 rating for time efficiency and a 4.84/5 rating for ease of use, indicating that digital systems substantially reduce the complexity of event coordination. Furthermore, evaluations based on the ISO/IEC 25010 standard highlighted strong system performance in reliability and functional suitability, reinforcing the effectiveness of centralized event management platforms in academic environments (Agpalo et al., 2025).

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates an Event Management System designed to strengthen the planning, coordination, and execution of activities among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The Events module centralizes event management by enabling officers to create and manage event details, organize schedules via the Activity Calendar, monitor event expenditures with the Event Budget Monitoring feature, and record participant attendance through digital verification and biometric authentication with the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader. To further improve planning efficiency, the system incorporates an AI-assisted Event Planning Assistant that utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API to generate structured event preparation plans, recommended timelines, logistics checklists, task lists, and planning guidance based on user-provided event information, including the event type, schedule, expected participants, and allocated budget. Automated notifications further support timely communication by delivering event reminders and updates to officers and participants throughout the event lifecycle.&nbsp;

**Biometric Identification Systems**

&nbsp;Manual sign-in procedures often compromise the reliability of campus attendance records due to proxy attendance, human error, and inefficiencies during high-volume student gatherings. Biometric Identification Systems address these challenges by utilizing unique biological identifiers to authenticate individuals in real time. Through this approach, institutions can streamline entry processes, reduce verification delays, and improve the accuracy of participation records. As a result, biometric attendance systems produce more consistent and verifiable attendance data while significantly reducing the administrative workload associated with manual verification.

&nbsp;Globally, studies have demonstrated that biometric technologies substantially enhance both the efficiency and reliability of attendance management systems. Obiora et al. (2025) found that implementing fingerprint-based biometric systems significantly improves operational efficiency by reducing attendance recording time from 22.25 seconds to 6.16 seconds per individual, representing a substantial increase in processing speed. The study further noted that biometric authentication reduces risks of impersonation and human error by ensuring secure, tamper-resistant identification records. These findings suggest that biometric systems contribute not only to faster processing but also to improved data integrity in institutional attendance management.

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, research indicates a strong acceptance and positive impact of biometric systems in academic environments. Katherine et al. (2023) reported that 92% of participants evaluated biometric attendance systems as effective and efficient in improving institutional processes, while 82% expressed positive perceptions regarding data privacy and system trustworthiness. These results highlight that biometric systems are not only operationally beneficial but also widely accepted by users, particularly when implemented with appropriate security measures. These findings reinforce the role of biometric technology as a practical solution for improving attendance management in educational institutions.

&nbsp;At the local level, findings from Cebu-based institutions further support the effectiveness of biometric systems in addressing attendance-related inefficiencies. A case study conducted at Cebu Technological University–Tuburan by Gabuya et al. (2022) revealed that biometric authentication significantly reduces processing time, averaging 1.82 seconds per verification. The study also observed that the system effectively eliminates long queues and delays commonly associated with manual attendance recording, thereby improving the overall efficiency of campus entry processes.

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates a Biometric Identification System to strengthen attendance management among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The system uses the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader to authenticate students' identities via real-time fingerprint verification, then automatically records attendance in the Events module. Verified attendance records are securely synchronized with the system's centralized database, enabling real-time monitoring, reporting, and auditability of event participation.&nbsp;

**Online Pre-Ordering System**

&nbsp;Integrating an online pre-ordering system into campus merchandise distribution is essential to enabling student organizations to efficiently manage high-demand item releases without logistical bottlenecks or delayed transaction processing. Effective pre-order management allows administrative officers to enforce strict fulfillment protocols while providing the student body with a fast, convenient, and structured reservation experience. This system of immediate token verification also minimizes unauthorized claims, prevents stock discrepancies, and reduces the risk of unexplained revenue leaks, thereby strengthening operational control and transparency.

&nbsp;Globally, industry data strongly supports the operational and user experience advantages of digital pre-ordering systems. A 2024 industry analysis examining the commercial impact of pre-order services found that digital claim systems fundamentally reshape user perception, where the process is viewed not merely as a transaction but as "buying convenient time" for oneself (Flipdish, 2024). The report further emphasized that online pre-ordering eliminates physical queues and restores user autonomy over ordering and claiming schedules. By reducing wait times and ensuring a structured retrieval process, organizations enhance user satisfaction, thereby increasing loyalty, retention, and overall system efficiency (Flipdish, 2024).

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, recent studies reflect a similar trend toward digital transformation as a driver of operational efficiency. A 2025 analysis of technology-driven business management in the Philippines found that adopting digital ordering and automated systems led to a 20% increase in service speed and a 10% reduction in overall operational costs (Savellano, 2025). These findings highlight that digital claim systems are not merely technological enhancements but strategic tools for managing high-volume demand and improving operational performance in local settings.

Within the local context, recent studies in Cebu likewise support the use of structured digital reservation and payment systems to improve transaction efficiency, monitoring, and user convenience. Capuyan et al. (2026) evaluated the online reservation system of Cebu Technological University–Danao Campus Facility Centrum and found that digital reservation features improved usability, streamlined the reservation process, enhanced monitoring, and supported more secure and efficient transaction handling. The study further emphasized the value of online reservation platforms in reducing transaction hassles, improving accessibility, and enabling administrators to monitor reservations more effectively. Complementing this, Abella et al. (2025) found that among digital payment users in Toledo City, Cebu, GCash was the most preferred platform for perceived usefulness, ease of use, attitude toward use, and behavioral intention to use. Together, these local findings suggest that integrating an online reservation mechanism with a widely accepted digital payment option can support faster, more organized, and more reliable transaction processing in Cebu-based settings.&nbsp;

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates an Online Pre-Ordering System to improve the distribution of merchandise among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The system enables students to reserve organizational merchandise online and choose between on-site payment or digital payment through GCash. For GCash transactions, students upload proof of payment, which is initially marked as pending until verified by an authorized officer. Officers validate the payment against the organization's GCash transaction records before confirming the order and recording the necessary payment details within the system. Upon successful verification, the student receives a unique tokenized digital claim code, which is presented during merchandise distribution to verify identity and order. The system further integrates a real-time order management dashboard that enables officers to monitor reservations, verify payments, manage order statuses, and efficiently oversee merchandise distribution.

**Inventory Management Systems**

&nbsp;Manual tracking errors, frequent stockouts, and inconsistencies in revenue recording often challenge the distribution of physical goods within campus organizations. Modern Inventory Management Systems mitigate these operational inefficiencies by implementing structured fulfillment verification protocols prior to item release and offering real-time visibility of stock levels. This approach enables more accurate inventory control, improves accountability, and reduces administrative errors in organizational distribution processes.

&nbsp;Globally, researchers have shown that web-based inventory platforms significantly enhance resource utilization and administrative reliability. In a 2023 study examining academic inventory systems, Ramos-Miller and Pacheco (2023) found that replacing legacy tracking methods with centralized digital platforms produced measurable improvements across key operational metrics. Specifically, the system resulted in an 85.51% increase in search efficiency, a 90.31% improvement in goods registration accuracy, and an 83.11% increase in report generation speed, culminating in an overall 86.31% improvement in inventory performance. These results demonstrate that centralized inventory systems reduce redundant processes while establishing a more reliable source of institutional data.

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, similar findings reinforce the value of digital inventory systems in improving organizational efficiency and decision-making. Tanaman et al. (2023) emphasized that automated inventory platforms function as powerful tools for making data-driven decisions, enhancing transparency and strengthening strategic oversight in resource management. These findings suggest that inventory digitalization is no longer merely a matter of operational convenience but a necessary framework for improving accuracy, accountability, and planning efficiency in institutional settings.

Within the local context, recent Cebu-based literature likewise underscores the value of structured inventory management in improving operational efficiency, stock monitoring, and accountability. Furtos (2026) assessed inventory management systems in cafés in Cebu City. They found that consistent inventory control procedures and monitoring were associated with stronger organizational performance, particularly in inventory speed, cost management, and accountability. The study further reported a very strong positive relationship between inventory management practices and inventory speed, as well as strong positive relationships with cost management and accountability. Although the study was conducted in a business setting rather than within student organizations, it remains relevant to the present study because it demonstrates, within the Cebu context, that systematic inventory monitoring and control mechanisms contribute to more efficient stock handling and more reliable operational oversight. These findings support the need for centralized inventory systems that provide accurate stock visibility, reduce administrative inconsistencies, and strengthen accountability in organizational distribution processes.&nbsp;

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates an Inventory Management System to strengthen the monitoring and management of organizational assets among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The system replaces fragmented manual inventory records with a centralized database that enables real-time tracking of stock levels, accurate item categorization, monitoring of inventory movements, and secure record management.

**Electronic Voting Systems**

&nbsp;Integrating secure digital voting mechanisms into campus governance is essential to enabling electoral committees to conduct fair, transparent democratic processes while mitigating vulnerabilities associated with traditional paper-based ballots. Effective electronic voting systems enforce single-vote authentication, employ tamper-resistant architectures to prevent data manipulation, and provide centralized candidate management to ensure procedural integrity. Additionally, features such as real-time vote counting and instant results dashboards reduce manual tallying errors and enhance electoral transparency, thereby strengthening trust in student governance and ensuring more efficient election processes.

&nbsp;Globally, research demonstrates that secure authentication protocols significantly enhance the integrity and reliability of electronic voting systems. A 2025 study by Tahir et al. found that implementing multi-layered authentication mechanisms, such as QR code verification, two-factor authentication (2FA), and one-time password (OTP) systems, substantially improves electoral security. The study reported a 98% authentication success rate and confirmed that such safeguards effectively prevent unauthorized access and multiple voting attempts. Furthermore, the system's ability to generate instant results eliminated delays and human errors associated with manual counting, with 95% of participants reporting improved security, usability, and reliability (Tahir et al., 2025). These findings highlight secure electronic voting systems as a critical component for ensuring transparent and fraud-resistant electoral processes.

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, organizations use digital voting platforms to improve transparency and strengthen student trust in electoral processes. A 2025 study by Tabanao and Cece demonstrated that transitioning from manual voting systems to a centralized electronic platform effectively addresses key vulnerabilities in traditional election procedures. The system achieved an overall rating of 4.39/5, with strong performance in accessibility (4.46/5) and reliability (4.41/5), indicating high user acceptance and system effectiveness. The study further emphasized that features such as audit-trail transparency and real-time result generation reduce the risk of vote manipulation and strengthen accountability in student elections (Tabanao & Cece, 2025).

Within the broader Visayas context, Drilon et al. (2026) developed and evaluated an Electronic Voting System for the Supreme Student Government of a maritime higher education institution in Negros Occidental. The researchers conducted the study to address the limitations of manual student elections, including time-consuming procedures, labor-intensive vote processing, counting errors, and security concerns. The researchers developed the system to automate the election process and evaluated it using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model to determine its efficiency, accuracy, reliability, and security. The findings support the use of centralized electronic voting platforms to streamline election administration, reduce manual tallying errors, strengthen voter verification, and improve the reliability of student governance elections.&nbsp;

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, HIUSA integrates an Electronic Voting System to strengthen the conduct of elections among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The system replaces fragmented manual voting procedures with a centralized digital voting platform that enables secure voting, authenticated voter verification, real-time tallying, and transparent result generation. By integrating the voting module with HIUSA's centralized student database, the system ensures that only eligible students can participate in elections while maintaining accurate and verifiable election records.

**Decision Support Systems**

&nbsp;Decision Support Systems (DSS) process and analyze organizational data to provide decision-makers with meaningful insights that support effective decision-making. Rather than replacing human judgment, DSS support informed decision-making by collecting, analyzing, and presenting relevant data to evaluate alternatives, identify trends, and provide evidence-based recommendations for organizational planning and management. In administrative and academic environments, these systems enable leaders to make more effective decisions by integrating analytical tools, real-time information, and structured decision-support mechanisms to address operational, financial, and logistical challenges.

&nbsp;Globally, recent literature highlights the significant role of Decision Support Systems in improving administrative efficiency and strategic planning. A 2025 study by Zangana and Salih found that DSS frameworks substantially enhance both the speed and accuracy of organizational decision-making by filtering and delivering relevant information for managerial use. The study further emphasized that such systems strengthen resource allocation processes and support proactive strategic planning, establishing a direct link between DSS implementation and improved organizational performance outcomes (Zangana & Salih, 2025). These findings indicate that DSS adoption is increasingly essential for organizations operating within complex, data-intensive environments.

Complementing this, a 2024 study by Nugraha and Onuegbu examining healthcare professionals' perspectives identified four primary benefits of DSS implementation: improved operational efficiency, enhanced decision-making accuracy, reduced operational costs, and increased user satisfaction. These findings reinforce the value of DSS in structured resource management, demonstrating its capacity to optimize operational workflows while improving cost-effectiveness and overall system performance (Nugraha & Onuegbu, 2024). Collectively, these studies highlight DSS as a critical tool for data-driven governance and resource optimization.

In the Philippine context, recent studies likewise demonstrate the value of Decision Support Systems in transforming institutional data into actionable insights to support more informed planning and management. Casildo et al. (2023) developed a Decision Support System to predict students' performance in the National Achievement Test using data from Central Mindanao University. They reported that the underlying Support Vector Machine model achieved an overall accuracy of 96% before deployment in the DSS. Their study shows that DSS can integrate institutional data, analytical models, and predictive outputs to support evidence-based academic interventions and more structured decision-making. Similarly, Secreto et al. (2025) found that academic administrators in the Philippines placed a high value on data-driven decision-making and strongly recognized the role of real-time monitoring in improving academic decision-making and achievement, while also noting the need for stronger information systems to support informed administrative decisions better. Together, these studies indicate that Philippine institutions increasingly rely on decision-support mechanisms to improve the quality, timeliness, and effectiveness of operational and strategic decisions.&nbsp;

Within the regional context, recent literature from the Visayas likewise demonstrates the relevance of Decision Support Systems in improving evidence-based governance and structured planning. Paculaba and Palaoag (2026) proposed a Geospatial Predictive Decision Support System for hazard risk profiling in Catbalogan City, Samar. They found that existing local government approaches remained limited by static data and weak decision-support capability. In response, their framework integrated geospatial datasets, predictive modeling, interactive visualization, and AI-assisted policy interpretation to strengthen risk assessment, resource allocation, and policy-oriented planning. Expert validation further confirmed the framework's conceptual relevance, usability, scalability, and innovation for local governance. Although the study focused on disaster risk management rather than student organization administration, it remains regionally relevant because it demonstrates that, within the Visayas, Decision Support Systems can consolidate complex data, generate actionable insights, and support more informed and systematic decision-making in organizational and governance contexts.

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates a Decision Support System to assist student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue in making informed operational and financial decisions. The system incorporates an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression model to forecast future financial trends; a Budget Advisory System that analyzes forecast outputs alongside current budget allocations and predefined financial rules to generate spending recommendations; and a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm to support the objective delegation of officer tasks. The system also incorporates an AI-assisted Event Planning Assistant that uses a Large Language Model (LLM) via the Groq API to generate structured guidance for event preparation based on user-provided event information. To improve transparency and user understanding, Hiusa further implements Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), which uses the LLM to translate AI-assisted forecasts, recommendations, and planning outputs into clear, human-readable explanations. Through these integrated decision-support capabilities, Hiusa enables officers and faculty advisers to transition from manual judgment to evidence-based decision-making, improving operational efficiency, resource management, and organizational governance.&nbsp;

**Workflow Automation Systems**

&nbsp;Transitioning from manual task assignment to an automated workflow infrastructure is essential for enabling student organizations to sustain high productivity and reduce administrative workload pressure. Effective workflow automation systems support intelligent task delegation based on officer roles and workload capacity, while also generating structured task lists and monitoring project deadlines. By minimizing repetitive coordination tasks and continuous manual follow-ups, these systems enable leadership teams to monitor organizational progress via a centralized dashboard, ensuring that complex activities are managed more efficiently and in a more organized manner from planning through completion.

&nbsp;Globally, recent literature emphasizes the importance of workflow automation systems in improving administrative efficiency within institutional environments. A 2023 study by Bhat on AI-powered workflow automation in higher education found that automated systems significantly reduce manual processing time, eliminate operational bottlenecks, and streamline administrative workflows. The study also found that automation enables personnel to shift their attention from repetitive administrative tasks to more strategic responsibilities, thereby enhancing overall productivity and operational agility (Bhat, 2023). These findings highlight workflow automation as a key mechanism for improving efficiency through structured process optimization.

In the Philippine context, similar findings reinforce the value of workflow automation in improving organizational performance. A 2024 study conducted in a government agency by Cabaobao et al. found that workflow automation tools significantly improve the speed, accuracy, and coordination of work processes. The study also confirmed that automating routine tasks enhances efficiency and reduces operational delays. However, it identified implementation challenges, including system integration issues and user resistance, that may affect adoption outcomes. Despite these limitations, the study concludes that workflow automation remains an effective framework for improving coordination and efficiency in complex administrative environments (Cabaobao et al., 2024).

Within the local context, recent Cebu-based literature likewise supports the use of automation technologies to improve process coordination, monitoring, and project efficiency. Ortiz et al. (2025) assessed the adoption and impact of construction automation technologies in Cebu City. They found that automation improves project management efficiency by enhancing coordination, supporting cost estimation, and enabling real-time monitoring of project activities. Their study further noted that despite implementation barriers such as regulatory gaps, limited financial capacity, and workforce readiness challenges, automation remains a valuable means of reducing procedural inefficiencies and strengthening the management of complex operational workflows.&nbsp;

In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates a Workflow Automation System designed to streamline the execution and monitoring of organizational processes among student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue. The system automates workflow generation for organizational activities, including events and administrative operations, by creating structured task sequences, monitoring deadlines, tracking task completion, and providing centralized visibility of ongoing processes. By working alongside Hiusa's decision-support capabilities, the system transforms recommended actions and assignments into organized workflows that officers can efficiently execute and monitor.&nbsp;

**Student Governance System**

&nbsp;Student governance systems play an essential role in improving the administration and management of student body organizations by providing a centralized platform for coordinating diverse organizational operations. By integrating key functions such as digital voting, financial management, event coordination, inventory monitoring, and workflow management, these systems reduce administrative fragmentation, improve operational transparency, and support data-informed decision-making. Through centralized access to organizational information and automated processes, student governance systems enable officers and advisers to manage responsibilities more efficiently while strengthening accountability and continuity within student organizations.&nbsp;&nbsp;

&nbsp;In the global context, studies on governance systems in educational institutions emphasize their significant role in improving organizational effectiveness and student-related outcomes. Sabas and Mokaya (2023) examined the influence of governance practices on students' performance in public secondary schools in Karatu District, Tanzania, focusing on participatory leadership, accountability, and transparency within school management systems. Using questionnaires and interviews analyzed through descriptive and correlation methods, the study found a strong positive relationship between governance mechanisms and academic performance, with participatory leadership (r \= 0.760), accountability (r \= 0.714), and transparency (r \= 0.512) all showing significant positive correlations with student outcomes. These results indicate that structured governance systems contribute to more effective decision-making, improved coordination, and enhanced organizational performance within educational environments. The findings further highlight that strengthening governance frameworks supports better management processes and more informed institutional decisions, aligning with Hiusa's objectives of promoting transparent, efficient, and data-driven student organization management systems.

&nbsp;In the Philippine context, researchers have developed student governance systems to improve the efficiency, transparency, and decision-making capabilities of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Arruejo and Arruejo (2024) developed and evaluated a Student Organizations Management System integrated with descriptive analytics and data visualization to support institutional decision-making. The system utilized a Rapid Application Development approach and a MySQL database backend to enable real-time monitoring of student organization activities and submission records. It also featured dashboards displaying Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), along with modules for document management, communication, and the dissemination of announcements to improve coordination between student organizations and administrators. Evaluation results showed a weighted mean of 4.43, interpreted as "Very Great Extent," indicating that the system was highly effective and suitable for implementation. These findings suggest that integrating digital governance systems in student organizations enhances administrative efficiency, strengthens transparency, and supports more informed and timely decision-making processes within HEIs (Arruejo & Arruejo, 2024).

Within the local context, recent literature from Cebu likewise highlights the importance of strengthening student governance structures to improve participation, representation, and organizational coordination. Tiongzon et al. (2024) examined the causes of student disengagement in student governance within the College of Arts and Sciences Student Body Organization at the University of Cebu–Main Campus. They found that a lack of connection, inequality in representation, faculty intervention, student unfamiliarity, feelings of being unrepresented, and unmet expectations contributed to student disengagement. These findings emphasize the need for governance mechanisms that improve communication, accessibility, and organizational coordination, highlighting the importance of digital platforms that can support student leaders in managing governance processes more effectively.&nbsp;

&nbsp;In alignment with these findings, Hiusa integrates a comprehensive Student Governance System that supports student body organizations at the University of Cebu Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue via a centralized digital platform. The system consolidates essential governance functions into interconnected modules, including an Electronic Voting System for secure elections, a Financial Information System for financial monitoring and reporting, an Event Management System for activity planning and coordination, and an Inventory Management System for resource tracking and management. It also incorporates a Biometric Identification System for secure event attendance verification and an Online Pre-Ordering System for organized merchandise reservation and distribution. Furthermore, Hiusa integrates Workflow Automation capabilities to streamline organizational processes and a Decision Support System that combines an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) forecasting model, Budget Advisory System, Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm, and Large Language Model (LLM) assisted features to support evidence-based planning, task delegation, financial guidance, and organizational decision-making.

### **Conceptual Framework**

![][image1]Figure 1: **Conceptual Framework of Hiusa**

&nbsp;The conceptual framework of Hiusa, illustrated in Figure 1, demonstrates how its governance modules and AI-assisted technologies interact to create an intelligent Student Governance System that enhances the administration of student body organizations (Sabas & Mokaya, 2023). Serving as the overarching framework, the Student Governance System integrates multiple organizational functions into a unified platform to improve transparency, accountability, operational efficiency, and evidence-based decision-making across student governance processes.

Hiusa integrates three core technologies to support its intelligent capabilities: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression (Hjalmarsson & Kiss, 2022), Rule-Based Decision-Making with Weighted Scoring (Zhu et al., 2022), and Large Language Models (LLMs) (Zhang et al., 2024). The OLS Linear Regression model analyzes historical transaction records to forecast future income and expense trends, supporting financial planning and the Budget Advisory System. The Rule-Based Weighted Scoring algorithm evaluates predefined organizational criteria, including officer roles, workload, task relevance, and availability, to recommend appropriate task assignments and improve workflow coordination. Meanwhile, the Groq-powered Large Language Model (LLM) supports AI-assisted announcement drafting, automatic generation of financial reports—including income statements, expense summaries, audit logs, financial summaries, and event-specific financial reports—AI-assisted event planning, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), which transforms the outputs of the OLS forecasting model, the Budget Advisory System, and the Rule-Based Weighted Scoring algorithm into clear, human-readable explanations that improve transparency and support informed organizational decision-making.

&nbsp;The platform supports organizational operations through three major governance domains. The Administrative and Governance Core facilitates leadership functions through the Electronic Voting System (Tahir et al., 2025), which enables secure electronic elections with authenticated voting, automated vote tallying, and digital election-result generation, together with the Decision Support System (Zangana & Salih, 2025), which provides analytical recommendations for financial planning, organizational management, and resource allocation. The Operations and Finance Management domain incorporates the Financial Information System (Uleh et al., 2025), which manages digital financial records, transaction monitoring, budget allocation, financial reporting, receipt verification, and the Automated Digital Ledger; the Inventory Management System (Ramos-Miller & Pacheco, 2023), which monitors organizational assets and merchandise inventory; and the Online Pre-Ordering System (Savellano, 2025), which enables students to reserve merchandise, submit GCash payment details for officer verification, receive digital claim tokens, and monitor order status. Meanwhile, the Events and Access Management domain integrates the Event Management System (Agpalo et al., 2025), which supports event scheduling, activity calendars, budget monitoring, notifications, attendance management, and AI-assisted event planning; the Biometric Identification System (Obiora et al., 2025), which utilizes the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader for real-time fingerprint authentication and attendance verification; and the Workflow Automation System (Bhat, 2023), which automatically generates organizational workflows, tracks task completion, and monitors operational deadlines.

Hiusa provides four distinct levels of system access: Student, SBO Officer, Administrator, and Department Head. Student users can participate in electronic voting, reserve organizational merchandise through the Online Pre-Ordering System, receive announcements and event notifications, and verify attendance during organizational activities using the DigitalPersona 4500 Fingerprint Reader. SBO Officers are responsible for carrying out assigned organizational responsibilities, including task execution, event coordination, attendance monitoring, merchandise distribution, and workflow participation while utilizing AI-assisted recommendations to improve operational efficiency. Administrator users, consisting of authorized student organization executives, manage organizational finances, events, elections, inventories, announcements, workflows, user accounts, approvals, and AI-assisted decision-support tools. They are also responsible for creating and managing SBO Officer and Department Head accounts, as well as maintaining organizational records and system configurations. Department Head users oversee organizational operations by reviewing financial reports, monitoring performance, evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and approving governance-related activities as required, thereby providing institutional oversight and accountability.&nbsp;

**Related Studies**&nbsp;  
&nbsp;This section reviews existing research on student governance systems, digital governance, financial administration, artificial intelligence, and institutional management technologies to establish the conceptual and technological foundation for developing Hiusa. The reviewed studies examine key frameworks and system architectures that support integrating centralized governance functions, intelligent decision support capabilities, and automated organizational processes into a unified platform. Specifically, the literature provides support for the implementation of financial information systems, event management systems, biometric identification systems, online pre-ordering systems, inventory management systems, electronic voting systems, workflow automation systems, and decision support systems, together with AI-assisted technologies such as financial forecasting, budget advisory, task delegation, event planning, and explainable artificial intelligence.

**Student Governance E-Voting Application for NORSU-Guihulngan Campus**&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;

&nbsp;Tabanao and Cece (2025) developed the Student Government E-Voting Application for Negros Oriental State University–Guihulngan Campus to enhance the efficiency, accessibility, security, and transparency of student government elections. The system replaces conventional paper-based voting with a centralized digital platform that enables eligible students to securely authenticate their identities, access electronic ballots, and cast their votes through a structured electoral process. It also automates vote counting and election result generation, significantly reducing the time, administrative effort, and human errors associated with manual election procedures. Furthermore, the application strengthens voter authentication, promotes election integrity, and improves the overall transparency and reliability of the student electoral process.&nbsp;

&nbsp;Similar to the Student Governance E-Voting Application, Hiusa supports student governance through a centralized digital platform that enhances the efficiency, transparency, and reliability of organizational elections. Both systems incorporate secure voter authentication, automated vote tallying, and digital election-result generation to improve the administration of student government elections while reducing reliance on manual processes. However, whereas the Student Government E-Voting Application focuses primarily on election management, Hiusa integrates the Electronic Voting System within a comprehensive student governance platform that also includes Financial Information Systems, Event Management Systems, Biometric Identification Systems, Online Pre-Ordering Systems, Inventory Management Systems, Workflow Automation Systems, and Decision Support Systems. Furthermore, HIUSA incorporates AI-assisted capabilities through Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression for financial forecasting, a Budget Advisory System for spending recommendations, a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm for SBO officer task delegation, and a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API for announcement drafting, financial report summarization, AI-assisted event planning, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI).&nbsp;

**UTHM Campus Event Management System**

&nbsp;Ainul Hisham and Mohd Zin (2025) developed the UTHM Campus Event Management System for Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia (UTHM) to improve the planning, coordination, and administration of campus events while increasing student engagement in organizational activities. The system addresses the limitations of the university's existing MyAktiviti portal by providing a centralized platform that enables students to access detailed information about student organizations, browse upcoming events, and register for campus activities. It also equips organizers with tools to manage event schedules, participant registration, and organizational information, thereby improving coordination and reducing the administrative burden of manual event management. Developed using the Prototype Model and evaluated through user-acceptance testing, the system achieved an overall satisfaction rate of 84.8%, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing event planning, organizational visibility, and stakeholder engagement within the university.

Similar to the UTHM Campus Event Management System, Hiusa supports student governance through a centralized Event Management System that improves the planning, coordination, and execution of organizational activities. Both systems provide a unified platform for managing events, maintaining organizational information, coordinating schedules, and improving communication between organizers and participants, thereby reducing reliance on fragmented manual processes. However, whereas the UTHM Campus Event Management System primarily focuses on campus event administration and student engagement, Hiusa integrates its Event Management System within a comprehensive student governance platform that also includes Financial Information Systems, Biometric Identification Systems, Online Pre-Ordering Systems, Inventory Management Systems, Electronic Voting Systems, Workflow Automation Systems, and Decision Support Systems. Furthermore, Hiusa enhances event management through AI-assisted capabilities by using a Large Language Model (LLM) via the Groq API to power an Event Planning Assistant that generates structured event-preparation plans, recommended timelines, resource suggestions, and task checklists based on user-provided event information.&nbsp;

&nbsp;**KDK College Canteen Ordering Portal**  
&nbsp;Kolte et al. (2025) developed the KDK College Canteen Ordering Portal for the canteen at KDK College of Engineering in Nagpur, Maharashtra, India, to improve the efficiency, convenience, and organization of on-campus food ordering and pickup operations. The system replaces conventional counter-based ordering with a centralized digital platform that allows students to scan QR codes displayed on tables or notice boards, browse available food items, place orders, and complete payments online. After students confirm their orders, the system automatically generates a unique digital token, which they present when collecting their purchases. Canteen personnel use the token to verify each transaction and prevent the release of incorrect or duplicate orders. The platform also enables administrators to update menu items, monitor incoming orders, track payments, and maintain transaction records. By supporting online pre-ordering, automatic token generation, and token verification, the system reduces queues, minimizes order-recording errors, accelerates service delivery, and improves the overall reliability of campus canteen operations.&nbsp;

&nbsp;Similar to the KDK College Canteen Ordering Portal, Hiusa supports digital pre-ordering through a centralized platform that streamlines reservation, payment verification, and merchandise distribution. Both systems enable users to reserve items online, generate unique digital claim tokens, and verify transactions before releasing products, reducing queues, minimizing manual errors, and improving the efficiency of distribution processes. However, whereas the KDK College Canteen Ordering Portal focuses primarily on campus food ordering and token-based pickup, Hiusa integrates its Online Pre-Ordering System within a comprehensive student governance platform that also includes Financial Information Systems, Event Management Systems, Biometric Identification Systems, Inventory Management Systems, Electronic Voting Systems, Workflow Automation Systems, and Decision Support Systems. Furthermore, Hiusa extends beyond conventional pre-ordering by incorporating AI-assisted capabilities, including Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression for financial forecasting, a Budget Advisory System for budget recommendations, a Rule-Based Weighted Scoring Algorithm for SBO officer task delegation, and a Large Language Model (LLM) accessed through the Groq API for announcement drafting, financial report summarization, AI-assisted event planning, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI).&nbsp;
